questions.stem: An 86-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-day history of cough, diagnosed in the emergency department as pneumonia. The patient's medical record includes a signed and notarized living will dated 2 years ago that indicates his desire for no cardiopulmonary resuscitation or ventilation in the event of incapacitation, and administration of comfort measures only. Upon admission, the patient requests full resuscitation if his status should decline. The patient is oriented to person, place, and time. Initially, only oxygen via nasal cannula and antibiotics are administered, but overnight the patient's status worsens. In the morning, pulse oximetry on 40% oxygen administered via face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 85%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: An 86-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-day history of cough, diagnosed in the emergency department as pneumonia. The patient's medical record includes a signed and notarized living will dated 2 years ago that indicates his desire for no cardiopulmonary resuscitation or ventilation in the event of incapacitation, and administration of comfort measures only. Upon admission, the patient requests full resuscitation if his status should decline. The patient is oriented to person, place, and time. Initially, only oxygen via nasal cannula and antibiotics are administered, but overnight the patient's status worsens. In the morning, pulse oximetry on 40% oxygen administered via face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 85%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Adhere to the living will and provide morphine for comfort
Ask the patient why his wishes changed
Contact the hospital ethics committee to provide guidance
Contact the patient's family to clarify his preferences
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Regardless of advance directives or prior code-status documentation, physicians need to assess all patients’ code status at each hospitalization, as the context of each hospitalization differs. The patient or the patient’s decision maker (eg, legal guardian or durable power of attorney) should be given the opportunity to update the patient’s code status. The patient expresses a preference to be full code, which signifies that life-prolonging care be administered while the patient is alive (eg, respiratory support, including with intubation, if lung function declines) and after the patient’s heart has stopped (eg, cardiopulmonary resuscitation). This preference supersedes his previously expressed preference for comfort care only, in which only medications that promote comfort are continued, while medications that solely prolong life are typically discontinued. Advance directives are legal documents that enable patients to dictate their preferences for end-of-life care ahead of time. Advance directives are especially important when patients become incapacitated and are no longer able to verbalize their wishes for care. However, capacitated patients can express wishes that supersede the preferences outlined in the advance directive, including preferences for code status. Since this patient is oriented and able to express a clear preference, the medical team should ventilate him, acting in accordance with his current wishes rather than his advance directive.

wrongAnswers.A: Adhere to the living will and provide morphine for comfort violates the patient’s autonomy. He appears capacitated and expresses a preference to change his code status to full code, which supersedes the advance directive. As such, the medical team should administer life-prolonging care by ventilating the patient. Ask the patient why his wishes changed (Choice B) is not the most urgent next step. It would be appropriate to ask this question while assessing the patient’s code status toward the beginning of hospitalization to determine the patient’s decision-making capacity to change his code status. However, asking this question in the current situation would delay needed respiratory support. Contacting the hospital ethics committee (Choice C) may be indicated if the patient’s current expressed wishes conflict with those previously stated and their decisional capacity is impaired. However, in this case, the patient is capacitated and clear in his preference to change his code status. Additionally, contacting the hospital ethics committee would delay appropriate emergency care that is required to sustain the patient’s life. Contact the patient's family to clarify his preferences (Choice D) would be an appropriate choice if the patient were incapacitated and did not possess an advance directive. However, in this case, consulting with the patient’s family is unnecessary. The patient is capacitated and clear in his preference to change his code status.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-week history of fever, sore throat, and diarrhea. The patient says that he was evaluated in an urgent care clinic 3 days ago; results of a rapid streptococcal test and heterophile antibody test for infectious mononucleosis obtained at that time were negative. Symptomatic treatment for viral respiratory infections was recommended, but the patient did not obtain any from his pharmacy. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. The patient reports that he has had oral-receptive and anal-receptive sex with men and that his most recent sexual encounter was 2 weeks ago. He does not use condoms. Today, temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows three oral ulcerations and anterior cervical lymph nodes that are slightly tender to palpation. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following studies is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

Which of the following studies is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
This patient with lymphadenopathy, fever, weight loss, and diarrhea most likely has acute HIV infection, known as acute retroviral syndrome. The presentation of primary HIV infection can vary significantly between patients, with some experiencing a mild febrile illness while others experience a severe, mononucleosis-like viral syndrome. The time between infection and onset of symptoms is variable, with incubation time lasting several weeks to months. During acute infection, there is a high degree of viral replication followed by widespread infection of CD4+ T-lymphocytes. The T-lymphocyte count may drop transiently, which is often normal in early HIV infections unless patients present with signs of opportunistic infection. Initial laboratory evaluation includes the use of a fourth generation HIV test, which tests for HIV p24 antigen and antibodies combined with direct measurement of the HIV viral load using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. It is common in early HIV infection for patients to have a negative fourth generation test but a high viral load; this is known as the window period. The window period varies depending on the kind of test used, including viral testing, though viral testing generally has the shortest window period and is therefore the most reliable test to detect infection. Once the diagnosis is made, laboratory studies should be sent for mutational analysis and

genotyping, but this should not delay the immediate institution of treatment with antiretroviral therapy. Therapy typically includes a combination of at least three different drugs from at least two different antiretroviral classes.

wrongAnswers.A: Epstein-Barr virus DNA detection and Epstein-Barr virus specific antibodies (Choice B) are not appropriate currently. While it is possible for this patient to have a previous false-negative heterophile-antibody test on prior testing, his overall clinical picture is more consistent with acute retroviral syndrome. Patients with acute mononucleosis will also have cervical lymphadenopathy, though oral ulcerations would be uncommon, and it would be expected that there will be some degree of splenomegaly on examination. HIV antibody testing (Choice C) is used in the setting of potential acute retroviral syndrome, though in the window period, may be falsely negative. The window period can be as many as 18 to 24 days from the time of exposure for antibody testing. While it can give insight into whether the patient has been previously exposed to HIV virus and in some cases can be positive, it does not provide information about the current severity of infection and is less accurate than assessing the viral load. Because of this, it is most appropriate to obtain a viral load at this time. Throat culture for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice E) is not the most appropriate next step. Patients with gonococcal pharyngitis can also present with fever and sore throat; however, it is not common for them to present with diarrhea and oral ulcerations, making it an unlikely diagnosis for this patient. Given the patient's sexual history and physical examination, acute retroviral syndrome is more likely. Throat culture for streptococcal pharyngitis (Choice F) is not warranted currently. This patient has been previously tested for streptococcal pharyngitis and was negative. While the result could have potentially been a false negative, erythematous, raised mucosa, and tonsillar inflammation would be expected on examination rather than oral ulcerations. Because of this, it is more appropriate to assess for HIV infection.

HIV antibody testing (Choice C) is used in the setting of potential acute retroviral syndrome, though in the window period, may be falsely negative. The window period can be as many as 18 to 24 days from the time of exposure for antibody testing. While it can give insight into whether the patient has been previously exposed to HIV virus and in some cases can be positive, it does not provide information about the current severity of infection and is less accurate than assessing the viral load. Because of this, it is most appropriate to obtain a viral load at this time. Throat culture for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Choice E) is not the most appropriate next step. Patients with gonococcal pharyngitis can also present with fever and sore throat; however, it is not common for them to present with diarrhea and oral ulcerations, making it an unlikely diagnosis for this patient. Given the patient's sexual history and physical examination, acute retroviral syndrome is more likely. Throat culture for streptococcal pharyngitis is not warranted currently. This patient has been previously tested for streptococcal pharyngitis and was negative. While the result could have potentially been a false negative, erythematous, raised mucosa, and tonsillar inflammation would be expected on examination rather than oral ulcerations. Because of this, it is more appropriate to assess for HIV infection.

explanationPanel.trap: HIV antibody and heterophile testing can be negative early; oral ulcers/diarrhea after high-risk exposure point to acute HIV.

questions.stem: During a routine health maintenance examination, a 15-year-old girl says that she has used marijuana with friends on four occasions. She is healthy and doing well in school. She requests that her parents not be told about the marijuana use. In addition to counseling her about the adverse effects of marijuana use, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention at this time?
questions.stemHtml: During a routine health maintenance examination, a 15-year-old girl says that she has used marijuana with friends on four occasions. She is healthy and doing well in school. She requests that her parents not be told about the marijuana use. In addition to counseling her about the adverse effects of marijuana use, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention at this time?
choices: Referral to a psychologist for treatment of substance use disorder
Scheduling a follow-up examination with the patient
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: C. Scheduling a follow-up examination with the patient
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Parental consent is required for most medical care of minors (patients younger than age 18 years). Exceptions include medical care related to sexual activities (eg, sexually transmitted infection, contraception, pregnancy care), substance use, and life-threatening medical or psychiatric conditions. (Emancipated minors may make their own medical decisions.) For these sensitive or time-sensitive issues, patient confidentiality and autonomy is favored over other ethical principles. Respecting a patient’s wishes about disclosure of medical information can build therapeutic alliance and increase the chance that patients will continue to share sensitive information in the future. As such, the physician should respect this patient’s wishes to keep her marijuana use confidential. The physician should establish regular follow-up visits to monitor for adverse consequences of marijuana use (eg, cognitive impairment, psychosis) and the development of a use disorder.

wrongAnswers.A: Referral to a psychologist for treatment of substance use disorder would be premature. This patient does not show signs of a use disorder, which commonly include using a substance more than planned, failed attempts to cut back use, and negative psychosocial consequences (eg, relationship conflict). The physician should monitor this patient longitudinally for the development of marijuana use disorder. Scheduling a family conference (Choice B) would oppose this patient’s wishes and violate the ethical principle of autonomy. From a legal standpoint, physicians do not need to
wrongAnswers.B: Referral to a psychologist for treatment of substance use disorder (Choice A) would be premature. This patient does not show signs of a use disorder, which commonly include using a substance more than planned, failed attempts to cut back use, and negative psychosocial consequences (eg, relationship conflict). The physician should monitor this patient longitudinally for the development of marijuana use disorder. Scheduling a family conference would oppose this patient’s wishes and violate the ethical principle of autonomy. From a legal standpoint, physicians do not need to
wrongAnswers.D: inform a patient’s parents about medical care related to substance use. Respecting this patient’s wish to not disclose her marijuana use to her parents would build therapeutic alliance. Screening for human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is not clinically indicated. HPV screening typically begins at age 25 years. Also, this patient’s marijuana use does not necessarily mean she is engaging in high-risk sexual activity. Urine toxicology screening (Choice E) may provide useful information about the full scope of the patient’s substance use in the future. However, this patient appears to be sharing honestly about her current substance use. Performing urine toxicology screening as a first step is likely to rupture the therapeutic relationship and decrease the chance this patient candidly shares sensitive information and collaborates in treatment planning in the future.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive pain and swelling of the left knee. She has pain with walking and at rest. There is no history of trauma. She has hypertension, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and asthma. Her current medications are insulin, a β-adrenergic blocking agent, and a daily inhaled corticosteroid. She is 158 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 136 kg (300 lb); BMI is 55 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.1°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. The knee is tender, swollen, warm, and erythematous. There is severe pain with passive and active range of motion. Plain x-rays of the knee show periarticular osteopenia; the joint space is narrowed medially. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Rheumatology

explanationPanel.correct: C. Aspiration of the knee joint
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Septic arthritis classically presents with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint along with systemic signs and symptoms of illness such as fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, and nausea. Septic arthritis results from a bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. The affected joint discloses pain upon passive range of motion, swelling, and erythema on physical examination. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically reveals purulent synovial fluid with greater than 50,000 leukocytes/mm³. Serum tests may also show leukocytosis and increased inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein concentration and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Treatment involves urgent intravenous antibiotics with patients often requiring surgical irrigation of the joint. In this case, the most likely diagnosis is septic arthritis because of the patient’s presentation of increased temperature and erythematous joint with pain upon passive range of motion in the absence of reported trauma. The most appropriate next step in management is aspiration of the knee joint to perform joint fluid analysis.

wrongAnswers.A: Measurement of serum uric acid concentration could be a reasonable step in
wrongAnswers.B: management in cases of suspected gout. Gout is an inflammatory arthropathy incited by hyperuricemia, with deposition of uric acid crystals inside the joint and surrounding tissues. Gout typically presents after consumption of a purine-rich meal or alcohol, which competes with renal excretion of uric acid. Microscopic examination of joint aspiration would typically show negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals and a leukocyte count less than 50,000/mm³. MRI of the knee can be useful in cases of traumatic injuries affecting the ligament, tendon, and/or meniscus of the knee. In this case, the patient did not sustain any trauma. Septic arthritis is the most likely diagnosis because of the patient's presentation of increased temperature, erythematous knee joint, and pain with passive range of motion. Aspiration of the knee joint is the most appropriate next step in management. Intra-articular injection of corticosteroid (Choice D) can be utilized in cases of knee osteoarthritis. In the setting of possible septic arthritis, intra-articular injection of corticosteroids is contraindicated. Further workup with aspiration of the knee joint is the most appropriate next step in management. Naproxen therapy (Choice E) may be a reasonable treatment option in acute gout or osteoarthritis. In this case, there is concern for septic arthritis. Joint aspiration with subsequent analysis of joint fluid is the most appropriate next step in management.

Microscopic examination of joint aspiration will classically disclose purulent synovial fluid with a leukocyte count greater than 50,000/mm³. This patient with progressive knee pain, increased temperature, and knee pain with passive range of motion in the absence of trauma, likely has septic arthritis. explanationPanel.trap: Do not inject steroids or give NSAIDs for presumed gout/OA before excluding an infected joint.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because of a 6-month history of daytime drowsiness. His wife reports that he has had increased snoring, which is especially loud when he sleeps on his back, but he does not stop breathing for prolonged periods. The patient has a 15-year history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows an increased intensity of the pulmonic component of S2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

His wife reports that he has had increased snoring, which is especially loud when he sleeps on his back, but he does not stop breathing for prolonged periods. The patient has a 15-year history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows an increased intensity of the pulmonic component of S2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Headaches that occur in the morning, daytime sleepiness, and loud snoring are frequently reported by patients with untreated obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This patient is likely experiencing sleep-related hypoventilation as a result of OSA. Clinical features of untreated OSA include excessive daytime fatigue, falling asleep at inappropriate times, loud snoring, and a disrupted sleep-wake cycle. Risk factors include male sex, obesity, congenital or traumatic anatomic abnormalities of the oropharynx and upper airway, neuromuscular disorders, and use of sedating medications. Untreated OSA is associated with hypertension. Diagnosis is made via polysomnography testing. Management consists of lifestyle changes (eg, weight loss, dietary modifications, increased activity, changing sleep position), avoiding sedating medications and substances, and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) while sleeping. Second-line therapies include oral appliances, such as mandibular advancement devices for symptoms refractory to CPAP use, and surgery for cases with obstructing lesions of the airway. Chronic, untreated OSA can result in pulmonary hypertension, which may manifest with heart murmurs or loud pulmonic heart sounds and eventual right-sided heart failure.

wrongAnswers.A: ECG is not the most appropriate next step in management. While the patient
wrongAnswers.B: has a history of hypertension and some cardiac risk factors, he has no symptoms that are indicative of cardiac origin. The loud pulmonic S2 is indicative of pulmonary hypertension likely caused by OSA. ECG would not be effective in diagnosing OSA in this patient, though it may show right-sided chamber hypertrophy. Echocardiography is not the most appropriate next step in management, though it may be indicated following polysomnography. This patient’s presentation raises suspicion for increased right-sided cardiac pressures, which would be diagnosed definitively with echocardiography, though he shows no other signs or symptoms at present. Patients with congestive heart failure have shortness of breath, edema, and potentially jugular venous distension. This patient does not display any of these symptoms or signs. Methylphenidate therapy (Choice C) or modafinil therapy (Choice D) are not commonly used for patients with daytime somnolence outside of narcolepsy or central apnea/injury. While methylphenidate or modafinil therapy is used to help wakefulness in the right patient population, such as some poststroke or traumatic brain injury patients, this would not address the underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms. Sleep positioning therapy (Choice F) may be an appropriate adjunct for this patient with likely OSA, but not prior to establishing the diagnosis. While this patient shows many signs and symptoms of OSA and positional sleep therapy may help, the severity of this patient’s OSA needs to be characterized to identify an appropriate treatment. For this reason, it is more appropriate to obtain a polysomnogram as the next step in management.

questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Primary hyperparathyroidism presents with hypercalcemia (which in turn presents with nephrolithiasis, chronic bone pain, abdominal discomfort, and psychiatric disturbances), hypophosphatemia, subperiosteal bone resorption, and end-stage kidney disease. Excessive production of parathyroid hormone results in increased serum calcium concentration from increased osteoclast activity, intestinal absorption, and renal tubular absorption. Serum phosphorus concentration is decreased secondary to increased

excretion by the renal tubules. Patients with laboratory findings consistent with hyperparathyroidism, such as this patient with hypercalcemia, should undergo further evaluation with the measurement of serum parathyroid hormone concentration. Once confirmed, imaging studies may localize a parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma.

wrongAnswers.A: Bone density test is not the most appropriate next step for this patient. While this patient does meet screening criteria for osteoporosis given her age and sex, a DEXA scan to evaluate her bone health will not lend information toward why she has an increased calcium concentration. Because of this, serum parathyroid hormone concentration should be assessed first. Renal ultrasonography (Choice B) is not necessary for this patient. This could lend information as to whether the patient has evidence of kidney disease, as a potential explanation for her increased creatinine concentration. However, measurement of serum parathyroid hormone concentration is more appropriate to assess the origin of her hypercalcemia, and additional testing could follow this if indicated. Urinary calcium concentration (Choice D) is not necessary currently. Patients with chronic kidney disease commonly have increased excretion of calcium in the urine as they are unable to resorb and maintain serum concentrations over time. However, this would not provide further diagnostic information about the underlying cause of her condition. X-ray of the spine (Choice E) is not appropriate at this time. Patients with multiple myeloma can have increased calcium, bone pain, anemia, and end-stage renal disease. X-ray of the spine can help assist in diagnosis and identification of lesions. However, it is more appropriate to assess this patient’s current parathyroid hormone concentration to identify the source of her hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 42-year-old man with a 1-month history of essential hypertension comes for a follow-up examination. He has been moderately obese for 20 years and follows a high-calorie, high-fat diet. He drinks four to five cups of coffee daily. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He drinks one beer at dinner almost daily. He has a sedentary lifestyle. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m². His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most effective method to decrease his blood pressure?

His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most effective method to decrease his blood pressure?
questions.subject: Cardiology

explanationPanel.correct: D. Weight loss of 9 kg (20 lb)
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Weight loss of 9 kg (20 lb) is the most effective intervention to decrease this patient’s blood pressure. On average, for patients who are overweight or diagnosed with obesity, the loss of 0.45 kg (1 lb) of body weight correlates with a drop in mean blood pressure by around 1 mm Hg. Continued aerobic exercise at least several times per week will also help reduce this patient’s blood pressure. Other interventions that are frequently helpful include dietary salt restriction, although many patients with essential hypertension will eventually require pharmacologic therapy to reduce their blood pressure below the current goal of 130/80 mm Hg. Particularly in young patients or those with ongoing hypertension despite the use of three medications including a diuretic, screening for causes of secondary hypertension should be considered.

wrongAnswers.A: Abstinence from alcohol is unlikely to have a meaningful effect on blood pressure in this patient who only drinks one beer daily. Male patients with hypertension who drink three or more drinks per day should be advised to reduce their intake to two or fewer drinks per day.
wrongAnswers.B: Abstinence from coffee is unlikely to affect this patient’s blood pressure in a significant manner. The association between caffeine intake and long-term blood pressure is unclear, but regular intake of coffee is not thought to contribute to the development of primary hypertension. There may be a transient increase in the patient’s blood pressure following consumption of caffeine; however, this will generally be brief and in temporal association with the duration of action of caffeine. Smoking cessation (Choice C) is unlikely to affect this patient’s blood pressure in the long term. Smoking has been shown to raise blood pressure transiently, while smoking the cigarette and in the minutes following, because of increased activation of the sympathetic nervous system. The effect on the blood pressure is transient with pressure returning to baseline within 10 to 15 minutes of finishing the cigarette. There has been no clear association between smoking and the development of chronic hypertension. Biofeedback (Choice E) is a mind-body technique that uses visual and/or auditory feedback in an attempt to gain control over involuntary bodily functions. It is not a proven means of reducing chronic hypertension. Vitamin E supplementation (Choice F) is unlikely to significantly affect this patient’s blood pressure. There is some evidence that vitamin E supplementation may cause a slight decrease in the systolic blood pressure of patients with mild hypertension, but no overall effect has been found on diastolic blood pressure or mean arterial pressure. The effect on systolic blood pressure is not as significant as is seen with weight loss.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She has osteoporosis treated with alendronate. She also takes a vitamin D supplement. The patient underwent a DEXA scan within the past year; she demonstrated a stable bone density with a T-score of -2.3. She is still active in her community, but she lives alone. BMI is 21 kg/m². She has never smoked cigarettes and does not drink alcoholic beverages. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. In addition to refilling her prescription for alendronate, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Depression screening is a routine preventive health measure recommended for all adults. However, elderly adults are under screened for depression. As depression is relatively prevalent in older adults and easily treatable, routine depression screening should occur. Other screening in elderly patients include screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65 to 75 years, breast cancer for women older than age 40 years with a life expectancy more than 5 years, and colorectal cancer for adults older than age 45 years with a life expectancy greater than 5 years. This patient is advanced in age, so cancer screenings are unlikely to be beneficial. Patients older than age 65 years should also be counseled about a healthy lifestyle, including regular aerobic exercise, a diet heavy in healthy fats, and smoking cessation.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of decreased appetite, nausea, and occasional vomiting. She also reports fullness and discomfort in her abdomen and abdominal cramps that have awakened her on several occasions. Her last bowel movement was 5 days ago and was characterized by loose stool. Thirty years ago, she underwent hysterectomy for leiomyomata uteri. She has a 10-year history of intermittent urinary incontinence. Her only medication is oxybutynin. Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities. She appears frail. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m². Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Examination shows warm, dry skin. The lungs are clear to auscultation and percussion. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs. The abdomen is soft and diffusely tender; there is no rebound or organomegaly. Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?

Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
questions.subject: Gastroenterology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Loose stool in the setting of hard stool in the rectal vault and increased stool burden suggests overflow diarrhea in the setting of severe constipation. Chronic, severe constipation with fecal impaction in the rectum can occur in the setting of decreased mobility, opiate use, or anticholinergic (eg, oxybutynin) use, which suppresses bowel peristalsis and increases the risk for constipation. This patient’s episode of loose stool occurred because only liquid can pass adjacent to the impacted stool. The first-line treatment for severe constipation with fecal impaction is administration of an enema. This works by introducing fluid into the large bowel, which serves to expand the intestinal tract lumen, soften the impacted stool, and stimulate peristalsis. Modification of risk factors should also occur, such as increasing fiber in the diet, limiting the use of opiate medications, or introducing stool softeners or osmotic agents into the medication regimen.

wrongAnswers.A: Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in a patient with a history of prior intra-abdominal surgery. Obstruction of the small bowel occurs from partial or complete blockage of the small bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, constipation, obstipation, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. This patient has a soft abdomen without distension, making small bowel obstruction less likely. Firm stool in the rectal vault is more suggestive of fecal impaction. Colon cancer (Choice B) most commonly occurs in the rectosigmoid region of the large bowel. Lesions within the ascending colon, by convention, typically result in slow bleeding, leading to iron deficiency anemia. Cancers within the descending and rectosigmoid colon are more likely to be infiltrative, resulting in obstruction of the large bowel. Patients may have thin-appearing stool. Loose stool with firm stool in the rectal vault is more suggestive of fecal impaction. In this patient with a normal colonoscopy 3 years ago, colon cancer so severe to cause constipation is unlikely. Diverticulitis (Choice C) presents with left lower quadrant abdominal pain, sometimes accompanied by diarrhea, fever, and tenderness to palpation over the left lower quadrant. It is less likely to present with constipation. This patient does not have fever or focal tenderness, and has diffuse abdominal tenderness, making diverticulitis less likely. Ischemic bowel (Choice E), such as with ischemic colitis, refers to inadequate blood supply to the colon, which can lead to bowel wall necrosis, loss of immune barriers, and bowel perforation. Ischemic colitis most commonly occurs in the setting of atherosclerosis, resulting in plaque rupture within a mesenteric vessel, systemic hypotension (eg, shock), or emboli such as in atrial fibrillation. Typical symptoms of patients with acute ischemic colitis include crampy abdominal pain, tenderness over the affected bowel, and hematochezia. This patient does not have focal tenderness, hematochezia, or risk factors for ischemic colitis, making this diagnosis less likely. Volvulus (Choice F) such as sigmoid volvulus results from twisting of the sigmoid mesentery, which can lead to large bowel obstruction and potential rupture or intestinal necrosis if not treated. It typically shows a coffee-bean appearance on abdominal x-rays. Sigmoid volvulus generally presents in an older patient with increasing abdominal distention, abdominal pain, constipation, and possible obstipation. This patient has a soft abdomen without distension and a sensation of fullness and discomfort, not severe abdominal pain, making sigmoid volvulus less likely.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up visit. He received the diagnosis of Chlamydia trachomatis infection 3 months ago. He was tested after his partner was found to be infected. The patient has never been symptomatic. He and his partner were treated with azithromycin. He has had five lifetime female sexual partners; he has used condoms inconsistently. He does not use illicit drugs. Examination shows no genital lesions. In addition to Neisseria gonorrhoeae and HIV testing, this patient should receive testing for which of the following sexually transmitted diseases?
questions.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up visit. He received the diagnosis of Chlamydia trachomatis infection 3 months ago. He was tested after his partner was found to be infected. The patient has never been symptomatic. He and his partner were treated with azithromycin. He has had five lifetime female sexual partners; he has used condoms inconsistently. He does not use illicit drugs. Examination shows no genital lesions. In addition to Neisseria gonorrhoeae and HIV testing, this patient should receive testing for which of the following sexually transmitted diseases?
questions.subject: Infectious Disease

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: This patient should receive testing for Chlamydia trachomatis given his history of previous infection and unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. C. trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents in men with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. For this reason, testing for C. trachomatis, as well as for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force for all sexually active patients under age 25 years. Complications of undiagnosed infection in men include epididymitis and reactive arthritis, as well as the possibility of further transmission to additional partners. Diagnosis is made with a nucleic acid amplification test, and treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection. The risk for reinfection in patients previously treated for C. trachomatis is high. As such, patients should be retested approximately 3 months after treatment to ensure their infection has resolved and they have not been reinfected.

wrongAnswers.B: Herpes simplex virus, type 1 is most commonly characterized by tender vesicles followed by ulceration and crusting, more frequently around the mouth, whereas herpes simplex virus, type 2 (Choice C) is more frequently characterized by similar lesions on the genitalia. Routine testing is less meaningful and not frequently performed, as many patients have positive serologic studies for herpes but no evidence of active or treatable infection. Human papillomavirus is a sexually transmitted viral infection that can cause cervical/vulvar and penile/anal carcinoma, as well as condyloma acuminata. Testing for human papillomavirus can be done in conjunction with Pap smear cytology in women but is not a part of routine diagnosis for active sexually transmitted infections, as many patients will have transient infections that clear on their own. questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension comes to the physician for a routine examination. Six months ago following a myocardial infarction, he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting that involved harvesting of the saphenous vein. He says he feels well. His medications are metformin, metoprolol, and lisinopril. Before his operation, he walked 3 miles daily; he has not resumed walking because he says he lacks the desire. On further questioning, he says he has not resumed any social activities because he feels tired on most days and does not want to leave his house. His blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg; other vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, there is lower extremity edema bilaterally, which is worse on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices: Administration of the Geriatric Depression Scale
Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities
questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.correct: A. Administration of the Geriatric Depression Scale
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: This patient is likely to meet criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD). Symptoms of MDD include 2 or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, decreased interest in exercising or socializing), guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor slowing or agitation, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (eg, decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. This patient demonstrates anhedonia and decreased energy despite his recovery from surgery several months ago. Though some patients are able to express a depressed mood, others (particularly men, patients over the age of 65 years, and African American patients) may not initially report a depressed mood and/or may present with primarily somatic symptoms. Treatment of MDD should include psychotherapy and antidepressant medication.

wrongAnswers.B: Determination of ankle brachial indices would assist in diagnosing peripheral artery disease (PAD). PAD commonly presents with extremity pain with activity and weak pulses. Edema, as seen in this patient, is uncommon. Also, this patient demonstrates a
wrongAnswers.C: constellation of symptoms consistent with MDD. Determination of erythrocyte sedimentation rate would assist in assessing for systemic inflammation. Though erythrocyte sedimentation rate is commonly measured in patients presenting with fatigue who have other focal symptoms that indicate an inflammatory process (eg, joint pain), this patient’s fatigue is likely caused by MDD as he has multiple symptoms suggestive of MDD. He does not report focal symptoms other than pedal edema, which is a known complication of coronary artery bypass surgery involving saphenous vein harvesting. Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities (Choice D) assists in diagnosing deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Symptoms and signs include unilateral lower extremity edema, skin pigmentation changes, pain, vein dilation, and venous ulcer formation. This patient shows bilateral pedal edema and lacks other typical signs of DVT. Fatigue and anhedonia are not common DVT symptoms. Echocardiography (Choice E) can be used to evaluate for systolic or diastolic dysfunction, intravascular volume status, and pericardial effusion. It is commonly used to determine the severity of a patient’s heart failure. Though bilateral pedal edema is a sign of heart failure exacerbation, this patient feels physically well and does not report symptoms of heart failure, such as dyspnea or orthopnea. His bilateral pedal edema is likely secondary to the coronary artery bypass surgery, as saphenous vein harvesting can lead to pedal edema. Also, he reports anhedonia, which is more consistent with MDD than congestive heart failure.

questions.stem: Of 65 men with coronary artery disease, 38 had an abnormal exercise stress test. Which of the following characteristics of screening tests does this demonstrate?
questions.stemHtml: Of 65 men with coronary artery disease, 38 had an abnormal exercise stress test. Which of the following characteristics of screening tests does this demonstrate?
choices: Predictive value of a positive test
questions.subject: Biostatistics/Epidemiology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Sensitivity is the ability of a test to detect a disease if it is present. A test is described as sensitive if it has a high likelihood of disease detection and, therefore, a low likelihood of a false negative (type 2 error). Given that the majority of patients with an abnormal exercise stress test have a history of coronary artery disease, the exercise stress test is a relatively sensitive measure of coronary artery disease. High sensitivity is therefore useful in ruling out a disease because a negative result indicates a very low likelihood that the disease is present. Because of this, high-sensitivity tests are useful for screening purposes in which proving the absence of disease and limiting the number of false-negative results are of the utmost importance. Sensitivity can be calculated by dividing true positives (TP) by the sum of TP and false negatives (FN), or TP/(TP + FN).

wrongAnswers.A: False-negative rate refers to the proportion of patients with negative stress tests who do in fact have coronary artery disease. Likelihood ratio (Choice B) is the ratio of false results to true results. Negative likelihood ratio is the ratio of false negatives to true negatives, while positive likelihood ratio is the ratio of false positives to true positives. This vignette does not describe false positives or negatives and instead identifies the proportion of true positives with a positive test result, which is consistent with sensitivity. Predictive value of a positive test (Choice C) is a statistical measure that defines the proportion of positive test results that are true positives (positive tests in patients who have the condition). Instead, this vignette describes the number of true positives (patients with coronary artery disease) who had positive test results. This is a separate concept more consistent with sensitivity.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She says that she began following a vegan diet (no dairy or animal products) 2 months ago. She takes no medications or dietary supplements. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Supplementation with which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She says that she began following a vegan diet (no dairy or animal products) 2 months ago. She takes no medications or dietary supplements. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Supplementation with which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: In this patient who has recently converted to a vegan diet, it is most appropriate to begin supplementation with calcium. Patients who follow vegan diets are at increased risk for deficiencies of iron, calcium, zinc, protein, fatty acids, and vitamin B12 (cobalamin). Given that these patients do not have consistent intake of these essential vitamins and minerals, it is appropriate to begin supplementation even prior to the emergence of any symptoms or signs of deficiency. In these patients, the low intake of dietary calcium increases the total body concentration of parathyroid hormone as well as vitamin D. This causes a reuptake of calcium from the bones to maintain appropriate serum concentrations. Over time, this can lead to low bone density and subsequent pathologic fractures.

wrongAnswers.B: Folic acid supplementation is not necessary at this time. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for folate deficiency. This is because high concentrations of folate can be found in green leafy vegetables, which the patient is regularly consuming. Magnesium (Choice C) supplementation is not necessary at this time. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for magnesium deficiency. This is because high concentrations of magnesium can be found in green leafy vegetables, beans, kale, spinach, bananas, and avocados.
wrongAnswers.C: Folic acid (Choice B) supplementation is not necessary at this time. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for folate deficiency. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for magnesium deficiency. This is because high concentrations of magnesium can be found in green leafy vegetables, beans, kale, spinach, bananas, and avocados.
wrongAnswers.D: Manganese supplementation is not necessary in this patient. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for manganese deficiency. This is because many foods that are part of these diets are high in manganese. Some examples of these are whole grains, quinoa, almonds, hazelnuts, chickpeas, spinach, and tofu. Vitamin A (Choice E) supplementation is not necessary in this patient. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for Vitamin A deficiency. This is because many foods that are part of these diets are high in Vitamin A, such as sweet potatoes, carrots, spinach, kale, squash, and cantaloupe.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has had an 8-day history of malaise, sore throat, nasal congestion, and rhinitis and a 2-day history of temperatures to 40°C (104°F), shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow mucus. She is alert and oriented. Her temperature is 39.7°C (103.4°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg. Breath sounds are decreased at the left apex posteriorly and anteriorly with increased tactile fremitus over that area. Inspiratory and expiratory crackles and rhonchi are heard. There is a normal S1 and S2 and no cyanosis, clubbing, or pedal edema. Her leukocyte count is 16,000/mm³. An x-ray of the chest shows a left upper lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus and is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia. Typical signs of pneumococcal pneumonia include fever, chills, productive cough, shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. Vital signs may show tachycardia and tachypnea. Physical examination may show rhonchi, crackles, decreased breath sounds, and increased tactile fremitus, such as in this patient. X-rays commonly show a lobar consolidation or, less commonly, bronchopneumonia. Management of community-acquired pneumonia includes antibiotics. Depending on severity and patient risk factors, the condition may require supplemental oxygen or mechanical respiratory support, intravenous antibiotics, and admission. Acute bacterial pneumonia may occur in isolation or following a viral respiratory syndrome, as in this case.

wrongAnswers.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis presents with hilar adenopathy and calcified pulmonary granulomas in primary infection. In reactivation, patients present with apical
wrongAnswers.B: pulmonary opacities and fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis. This patient does not have night sweats or risk factors for tuberculosis infection, making this an unlikely causal organism. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an atypical organism that can cause pneumonia, which usually presents with fevers, cough, and infiltrates on chest x-ray. Clinical examination findings typically show abnormal breath sounds. It is a common atypical bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia in young adults, resulting in the development of alveolar and interstitial infiltrates on chest imaging. This patient has a lobar infiltrate on chest imaging, making S. pneumoniae the most likely causal organism. Neisseria meningitidis (Choice C) infection usually causes meningococcemia or meningitis. It typically presents acutely with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, myalgias, and a diffuse petechial rash. It can quickly evolve to florid shock accompanied by disseminated intravascular coagulation. This patient has pneumonia, making S. pneumoniae the most likely causal organism. Pneumocystis jiroveci (Choice D) is a common opportunistic cause of pneumonia in patients with late-stage HIV infection and/or AIDS2. It is a yeast-like fungal organism that can cause pneumonia in immunocompromised patients. Chest imaging typically shows diffuse, bilateral infiltrates often prominently about the hila. This patient is not immunocompromised and has lobar pneumonia, making P. jiroveci an unlikely causal organism. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice E) is a gram-negative rod that causes a variety of infections, including pneumonia and bacteremia. It is more associated with hospital-acquired or ventilator-acquired pneumonia. This patient does not have a history of hospitalization or ventilation, so P. aeruginosa is a less likely causal organism. S. pneumoniae is the most likely causal organism for community-acquired pneumonia. Respiratory syncytial virus (Choice F) and rhinovirus (Choice G) commonly result in acute bronchiolitis in children or an upper respiratory tract infection in adults. Pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus or rhinovirus is usually an atypical pneumonia with diffuse opacities. This patient has a lobar consolidation, making a bacterial cause more likely.

It typically presents acutely with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, myalgias, and a diffuse petechial rash. It can quickly evolve to florid shock accompanied by disseminated intravascular coagulation. This patient has pneumonia, making S. pneumoniae the most likely causal organism. Pneumocystis jiroveci (Choice D) is a common opportunistic cause of pneumonia in patients with late-stage HIV infection and/or AIDS2. It is a yeast-like fungal organism that can cause pneumonia in immunocompromised patients. Chest imaging typically shows diffuse, bilateral infiltrates often prominently about the hila. This patient is not immunocompromised and has lobar pneumonia, making P. jiroveci an unlikely causal organism. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice E) is a gram-negative rod that causes a variety of infections, including pneumonia and bacteremia. It is more associated with hospital-acquired or ventilator-acquired pneumonia. This patient does not have a history of hospitalization or ventilation, so P. aeruginosa is a less likely causal organism. S. pneumoniae is the most likely causal organism for community-acquired pneumonia. Respiratory syncytial virus (Choice F) and rhinovirus commonly result in acute bronchiolitis in children or an upper respiratory tract infection in adults. Pneumonia caused by respiratory syncytial virus or rhinovirus is usually an atypical pneumonia with diffuse opacities. This patient has a lobar consolidation, making a bacterial cause more likely.

explanationPanel.rule: Lobar consolidation after viral URI with fever/productive cough is classic community-acquired Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with gout has the sudden onset of extreme pain, swelling, and exquisite tenderness of the right knee; he cannot bear the pressure of wearing slacks. He has not recently taken any medication and previously had intractable diarrhea while taking colchicine. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for treating this acute episode?

He has not recently taken any medication and previously had intractable diarrhea while taking colchicine. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for treating this acute episode?
questions.subject: Rheumatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Gout is an acute, monoarticular arthropathy resulting from an intra-articular inflammatory reaction to precipitation of monosodium urate crystals. Deposition of uric acid crystals may occur in the surrounding tissues, leading to the development of tophi. Gout typically presents with atraumatic joint pain, erythema, and swelling. The most common joint involved is the first metatarsophalangeal, but other common joints include the knees and elbows. Increased intake of foods that are rich in purines such as seafood and red meats have been shown to increase the risk for gout flares, as they result in increased production of uric acid. Other causes of increased uric acid concentration include diuretic use, tumor lysis syndrome, alcohol consumption, and obesity. Arthrocentesis is performed and microscopic examination of the synovial fluid generally shows a leukocyte count of 10,000–50,000/mm³ with a mixture of neutrophils and lymphocytes, and needle-like, birefringent crystals. Treatment of an acute flare consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as naproxen or indomethacin as well as colchicine, or corticosteroids. In this case, the patient is most likely presenting with a gout flare because of the sudden onset of his symptoms. The most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy is indomethacin for this patient who previously did not tolerate colchicine.

wrongAnswers.A: Allopurinol and probenecid (Choice E) are both urate-lowering medications. Allopurinol functions by inhibiting xanthine oxidase and probenecid functions by decreasing the reabsorption of urate. These medications are important pharmaceutical options in preventing gout flares. In this case, the patient is presenting with an acute gout
wrongAnswers.B: flare and the most appropriate drug for treatment is indomethacin. Codeine is an opiate medication used for pain management or cough in a select group of patients. In cases of acute gout flares, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and/or corticosteroids are the first-line treatments for pain relief and management. Indomethacin would be the most appropriate drug for treating this acute gout flare.
wrongAnswers.D: Prednisone is often not the most recommended initial therapy for the treatment of an acute gout flare. Because of its side effect profile, most clinicians recommend the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or colchicine initially. While corticosteroids can be given for acute gout flares, these other medications are typically administered first.

These medications are important pharmaceutical options in preventing gout flares. In this case, the patient is presenting with an acute gout

questions.stem: A 72-year-old African American man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of mild, vague abdominal pain. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and osteoarthritis of the knees. His medications are lisinopril, metformin, and acetaminophen. He does not smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs. He drinks eight glasses of wine weekly. He is a retired hotel desk clerk. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 79 kg (175 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 156/97 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a pulsatile midline mass 7 cm above the umbilicus. No other abnormalities are noted. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin A1c of 8.4% and serum total cholesterol concentration of 260 mg/dL. Which of the following factors is most predictive of future complications of this patient’s condition?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: This older patient with a pulsatile abdominal mass has examination findings consistent with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). AAAs are most commonly seen in male smokers with a family or personal history of atherosclerotic disease. They commonly occur in the infrarenal abdominal aorta and may present as a palpable, pulsatile abdominal mass if the aneurysm is large and the patient is a healthy weight. Smoking is the modifiable risk factor most strongly associated with both development of an AAA as well as its expansion and rupture. Uncontrolled hypertension has been shown to be associated with increased rate of expansion and rupture as well, although the association is less strong. Ruptured aneurysms require emergent surgical intervention and repair. Chronic aneurysms are typically asymptomatic. The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends using ultrasonography to screen for AAA in men age 65 to 75 years who have a history of tobacco use.

wrongAnswers.A: Alcohol consumption has variable effects on AAA development. Small amounts of moderate alcohol consumption have been shown to reduce risk for AAA development,
wrongAnswers.C: while high levels (more than 2 drinks/day) of alcohol consumption may slightly increase the risk. This patient has a moderate level of alcohol consumption, which would not contribute to his risk for developing an AAA and may even be protective. Alcohol consumption has not been shown to affect the rate of AAA rupture. Ethnicity has been associated with the prevalence of AAA, but not with risk for rupture or expansion. AAAs develop most frequently in White patients; however, AAA can develop in patients of any ethnicity. Diabetes is associated with a lower risk for the development of an AAA, as well as AAA expansion and rupture. questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of frequent loss of urine. During this time, she has had loss of urine at rest and with activity. She wears an absorbent pad each night; it is soaked by morning. She has difficulty initiating her urinary stream, which is weak. She has had six urinary tract infections during the past year. She has had type 1 diabetes mellitus since the age of 6 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A cough stress test is positive. Her postvoid residual volume is 800 mL. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

She wears an absorbent pad each night; it is soaked by morning. She has difficulty initiating her urinary stream, which is weak. She has had six urinary tract infections during the past year. She has had type 1 diabetes mellitus since the age of 6 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A cough stress test is positive. Her postvoid residual volume is 800 mL. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Overflow incontinence occurs when bladder emptying is impaired, eventually resulting in intravesical hydrostatic pressure overcoming internal and external urinary sphincter closing pressures, thereby causing the leakage of urine. It can occur due to a variety of causes, including neurologic insults (eg, diabetic neuropathy, stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis) that result in bladder atony, and bladder outlet obstruction secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia or a bladder mass. This patient’s long history of type 1 diabetes mellitus increases her risk for diabetic neuropathy and overflow incontinence secondary to neurogenic bladder. Patients develop urinary retention with an inability to void and may have loss of urine with Valsalva maneuver or increased abdominopelvic pressure. The diagnosis is established with a urodynamic study, which typically shows an increased postvoid residual volume, such as in this patient with a postvoid residual volume of 800 mL. In contrast to an overactive bladder, which is treated with oxybutynin, overflow incontinence is treated with bethanechol, a muscarinic agent that promotes bladder contraction, or with intermittent catheterization.

wrongAnswers.A: Functional incontinence describes incontinence secondary to external factors or another condition creating inability to void in a timely manner or inability to recognize
wrongAnswers.C: the need to void. Several causes of functional incontinence include cognitive disorders such as dementia, movement disorders such as multiple sclerosis or Parkinson disease, physical barriers, or medication effect. This patient has no evidence of a secondary cause of incontinence. Rather, she shows signs of a primary cause of incontinence, overflow incontinence, as evidenced by increased postvoid residual volume. Stress incontinence is incontinence that is triggered by an increase in intra-abdominal pressure (eg, lifting, sneezing, Valsalva maneuver). Stress incontinence results from urethral hypermobility caused by pelvic floor weakness/prolapse or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. Urethral hypermobility is evidenced on physical examination by deviation greater than 30 degrees from the horizontal of an inserted cotton-tipped applicator with straining. This patient’s physical examination is normal, making stress incontinence less likely. In addition, stress incontinence would not have increased postvoid residual volume, which is more suggestive of overflow incontinence. Risk factors for stress incontinence include multiple vaginal deliveries, obesity, and prostate surgery. Urge incontinence (Choice D), or overactive bladder with incontinence, is caused by detrusor muscle instability and commonly presents with the urge to void followed shortly by the leakage of urine. Patients would have low postvoid residual volume, in contrast with overflow incontinence such as in this patient. Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic medication used to treat urge incontinence from an overactive bladder and detrusor instability. Urinary tract infection (Choice E) can present with an overactive bladder (frequency, urgency, urge incontinence). Patients generally also experience dysuria and suprapubic pain. The presence of bacteria and white blood cells on urinalysis is typical. This patient has no dysuria and a normal urinalysis, making urinary tract infection unlikely. Vesicovaginal fistula (Choice F) can be a consequence of gynecologic surgery, pelvic malignancy, or radiation therapy. It typically presents with painless urinary leakage from the bladder into the vagina. On pelvic examination, a pool of urine is typically present in the vaginal canal. This patient’s physical examination shows no abnormalities, making vesicovaginal fistula less likely.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She says she feels well. She has no history of serious illness or sexually transmitted infection. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive, for which she requests a refill. She has had five lifetime sexual partners. During the past 4 months, she has been monogamous with one male partner. She has never used condoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. In addition to refilling the oral contraceptive prescription, which of the following is the most appropriate screening for cervical cancer?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She says she feels well. She has no history of serious illness or sexually transmitted infection. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive, for which she requests a refill. She has had five lifetime sexual partners. During the past 4 months, she has been monogamous with one male partner. She has never used condoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. In addition to refilling the oral contraceptive prescription, which of the following is the most appropriate screening for cervical cancer?
choices: Pap smear and high-risk HPV genotyping
Pap smear with reflex HPV testing
No screening is indicated at this time
questions.subject: Gynecology

explanationPanel.correct: E. No screening is indicated at this time
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: No cervical cancer screening is indicated at this time given this patient’s age. Pap smear testing uses a cervical swab to collect cells from the transformation zone of the cervix and is an important screening tool for the detection of cervical carcinoma. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines recommend screening for cervical carcinoma with Pap smear testing every 3 years between ages 21 and 29 years, and Pap smear screening every 5 years with co-testing for human papillomavirus (HPV) or every 3 years with Pap smear testing alone between ages 30 and 65 years. Screening is not recommended before age 21 years. However, this patient should undergo appropriate screening for sexually transmitted infections, such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, given her history of unprotected intercourse with multiple prior partners.

wrongAnswers.A: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) genotyping only is not recommended as a screening modality for sexually transmitted infections or cervical cancer. The strains most commonly implicated in condyloma acuminata are HPV 6 and 11, whereas those that confer the highest risk for progression to cervical cancer include strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. Screening in asymptomatic patients is not recommended as infections are typically transient and may be cleared by the patient’s immune system.
wrongAnswers.B: Pap smear and high-risk HPV genotyping is not recommended for this patient. Pap smear and high-risk HPV genotyping is typically reserved as a cervical cancer screening modality for patients between ages 30 and 65 years. Screening is not recommended in patients under age 21 years. Pap smear with reflex HPV testing (Choice C) is not recommended for this patient. Clinicians may choose to perform reflex HPV testing if the result of cytology is abnormal to further delineate the risk for cervical cancer. However, neither of these tests are recommended in patients under age 21 years. Paper smear only (Choice D) is not recommended by the USPSTF for patients under age 21 years. The risks of screening and additional testing typically outweigh the benefits in this population.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman, who was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 1 month ago, comes to the office as a new patient. She recently moved to the area. The diagnosis was made based on a 2-week history of excessive urination and a nonfasting serum glucose concentration of 225 mg/dL. She is currently asymptomatic. She has no other history of serious illness. Her only medication is metformin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Today, her hemoglobin A1c is 6.1%, and nonfasting serum glucose concentration is 135 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient to prevent disease-related morbidity?

She has no other history of serious illness. Her only medication is metformin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Today, her hemoglobin A1c is 6.1%, and nonfasting serum glucose concentration is 135 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient to prevent disease-related morbidity?
questions.subject: Endocrinology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: The 2023 United States Preventive Services Task Force guidelines recommend various screening tests and interventions for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Comprehensive eye examination, foot examination, major depressive disorder screening, weight management counseling, and tobacco cessation counseling are recommended annually. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus should also be screened for high blood pressure at every medical visit. Lipid profile screening should be done at least every 5 years to measure total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides concentrations. Annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio test and blood test to measure serum creatinine concentration should be performed to detect early-stage kidney disease. Guidelines may need to be individualized based on a patient's specific clinical characteristics and comorbidities.

wrongAnswers.B: Exercise stress test is not appropriate for this patient. While patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus do have increased risk for cardiovascular disease, this patient shows no signs or symptoms of this. Additionally, this patient has no complaints of chest pain, nor ECG findings that would be suggestive of unstable angina or any type of occlusive coronary lesion.
wrongAnswers.C: Herpes zoster vaccination is not necessary for this patient. Herpes zoster vaccination is recommended for immunocompetent individuals over the age of 50. Given the patient's age and lack of history of HIV, cancer, or autoimmune disease, this is not yet required. Monthly determination of hemoglobin A1c (Choice D) is not appropriate. Hemoglobin A1c is a measurement of average glycosylation of red blood cells (RBCs). Given that the average lifespan of RBCs is 90-120 days, it gives a reliable estimate of average blood glucose concentration over the preceding three months. Monthly checks are not appropriate, even in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Pneumococcal vaccination (Choice E) is not necessary for this patient. Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for patients over the age of 65 or for patients who are asplenic. Given this patient’s age and lack of history of splenectomy, this is incorrect.
wrongAnswers.D: Herpes zoster vaccination (Choice C) is not necessary for this patient. Herpes zoster vaccination is recommended for immunocompetent individuals over the age of 50. Lipid profile screening should be performed at least every 5 years. Routine screening of hemoglobin A1c should occur every 3 months. These recommendations are based on 2023 United States Preventive Services Task Force guidelines.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 6-month history of moderate right upper abdominal pain that occurs 15 to 60 minutes after he eats. The episodes occur once or twice weekly and resolve in less than 1 hour. He otherwise is asymptomatic. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. His mother says he eats three fast-food meals weekly. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is nontender. The spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows 20 gallstones measuring 3 mm to 10 mm. His hemoglobin concentration is 7.7 g/dL (N=11.5–14.5). A blood smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

A blood smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
choices: Change in the shape of red blood cells
Production of autoantibodies directed against the red blood cell membrane
Switch from glutamic acid to valine in the globin chain
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.correct: A. Change in the shape of red blood cells
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is a disorder of red blood cell membrane proteins that limits the ability of the cell to conform when passing through narrow capillary beds. This results in early removal of the red blood cells by the spleen and a resultant hemolysis, which causes normocytic, hemolytic anemia. HS is the most common disorder of the red blood cell membrane and is frequently seen in people of European descent. A family history of HS is generally present. Autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins cause HS through loss of the normal connection between the inner membrane skeleton and the outer lipid bilayer. Patients typically present with fatigue, global weakness, and pallor, with associated splenomegaly and jaundice on physical examination. Laboratory studies generally show anemia and indirect hyperbilirubinemia along with an abnormal osmotic fragility test and eosin-5’-maleimide analysis on flow cytometry. Patients are prone to development of bilirubin gallstones because of the high levels of indirect bilirubin. Blood smear shows rounded red blood cells without central pallor. Splenic congestion and sequestration are hallmarks of moderate -to -severe disease. Splenectomy is indicated to reduce the degree of premature red blood cell consumption (ie, extravascular hemolysis) and the risk for sequestration crises.

wrongAnswers.B: A fat-rich diet is not the most likely cause. While this patient does have evidence of cholelithiasis, which can then precipitate pain after fatty meals, he also has 20 gallstones which is significantly abnormal. In addition, this patient has spherocytes on blood smear and splenomegaly, neither of which can be attributed to a fat-rich diet. Presence of antiplatelet IgG antibodies (Choice C) is seen in immune thrombocytopenia, which results from the immune-mediated destruction of circulating platelets. It presents with thrombocytopenia, mucosal bleeding, and petechiae or purpura from cutaneous hemorrhage. Platelets and erythrocytes appear normal on peripheral smear, making this answer unlikely. Production of autoantibodies directed against the red blood cell membrane (Choice D) is seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is a type II (complement-mediated cytotoxicity) hypersensitivity reaction in which autoantibodies form to antigens on the surface of erythrocytes. Antibody binding to these antigens causes the erythrocytes to be targeted for destruction by complement, leading to the breakdown of erythrocytes (ie, hemolysis). Hemolysis leads to the release and subsequent degradation of hemoglobin, a byproduct of which is bilirubin. Spherocytes would not be expected in patients with autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Switch from glutamic acid to valine in the globin chain (Choice E) is characteristic of sickle cell disease. Sickle cell disease results from a single amino acid substitution in the β-globin gene that leads to production of an abnormally shaped β-globin molecule and formation of abnormal hemoglobin S, which polymerizes abnormally in the setting of hypoxia and causes sickling of erythrocytes. Spherocytes would not be expected in a patient with sickle cell disease.
