questions.stem: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of a nonitchy, painless, gradually enlarging lesion on his face that he first noticed 6 months ago. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of a nonitchy, painless, gradually enlarging lesion on his face that he first noticed 6 months ago. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common subtype of skin cancer and is associated with ultraviolet (UV) exposure. Basal cell carcinoma clinically presents as a pearly papule with rolled borders, overlying telangiectasia, and may have focal erosion or ulceration. Patients often describe this lesion as “the pimple that will not pop” or “the wound that will not heal.” Basal cell carcinoma can be locally invasive; however, metastasis is rare. Clinical subtypes of basal cell carcinoma include superficial, nodular, pigmented, microcystic, and morpheaform type. Basal cell carcinoma pathology will show islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, and retraction from the surrounding dermis. Treatment for basal cell carcinoma includes excision such as Mohs micrographic surgery, electrodessication and curettage, or topical imiquimod therapy. This patient’s presentation and the photograph shown are consistent with basal cell carcinoma.

wrongAnswers.A: Actinic keratoses are associated with UV damage and are found on sun-exposed sites including the face, ears, neck, and extremities. Actinic keratoses result from partial-thickness epidermal atypia, which may progress to squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated. Physical examination discloses ill-defined, rough, scaly papules. Actinic keratoses are treated with cryotherapy, topical fluorouracil, and topical imiquimod. While actinic keratoses are associated with UV damage, this case is more consistent with basal cell carcinoma. Keratoacanthoma (Choice C) is considered a variant of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Keratoacanthoma clinically presents as a rapidly enlarging, crateriform nodule, with a central hyperkeratotic core. Keratoacanthoma, unlike squamous cell carcinoma, may involute over a period of months, leaving behind a scar. While some lesions spontaneously resolve, biopsy is recommended to rule out invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Keratoacanthoma usually shows rapid growth, unlike a slow growing basal cell carcinoma. Seborrheic keratosis (Choice D) is a common benign growth, found in middle-aged and elderly adults. They commonly present as brown, sharply demarcated papules in sun-exposed sites. Seborrheic keratoses do not represent melanocytic growths, but are related to a thickening of the epidermis, pigment deposition, and development of intraepidermal keratin cysts. Patients should be provided reassurance. Seborrheic keratoses may be clinically monitored. Squamous cell carcinoma (Choice E) is the second most common form of skin cancer and is associated with chronic sun exposure. UV damage over time leads to the development of thymidine dimers and mutations in p53, a tumor suppressor gene. Squamous cell carcinoma clinically presents as a chronic, rough, eroded papule or nodule, with an overlying hyperkeratotic crust. Lesions suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma warrant biopsy, and treatment modalities include standard excision, Mohs micrographic surgery, and electrodessication and curettage. This case is consistent with basal cell carcinoma, as opposed to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 3-week history of nausea without associated vomiting. The patient's mother waits outside the examination room during the evaluation. The patient has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Since menarche at age 11 years, her menstrual periods have occurred at irregular 30- to 60-day intervals; her last menstrual period was 2 months ago. The patient reports that she has been dating her 18-year-old boyfriend for the past 5 months; they are sexually active and use condoms inconsistently. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urine pregnancy test is positive. While discussing the results with the patient, she states that she does not know what to do. Which of the following is the most important question for the physician to ask the patient during the conversation?
questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 3-week history of nausea without associated vomiting. The patient's mother waits outside the examination room during the evaluation. The patient has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Since menarche at age 11 years, her menstrual periods have occurred at irregular 30- to 60-day intervals; her last menstrual period was 2 months ago. The patient reports that she has been dating her 18-year-old boyfriend for the past 5 months; they are sexually active and use condoms inconsistently. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urine pregnancy test is positive. While discussing the results with the patient, she states that she does not know what to do. Which of the following is the most important question for the physician to ask the patient during the conversation?
choices: "Do you want me to contact child protective services?"
"Have you considered placing the child up for adoption?"
"How do you think your boyfriend will react to this news?"
"Is this a situation we could discuss with your mother?"
"Would you like a confidential referral to discuss abortion services?"
questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: D. "Is this a situation we could discuss with your mother?"
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Parental consent is required for most medical care of minors (patients younger than 18 years). Exceptions include medical care related to sexual health (eg, pregnancy care, sexually transmitted infection, contraception), substance use, and life-threatening medical or psychiatric conditions. For these sensitive or time-sensitive issues, patient confidentiality and autonomy is favored over other ethical principles. This minor patient who is pregnant has challenging decisions to make. The physician’s role is to discuss the options and facilitate informed and thoughtful decisions. She should be asked whether she wants her parents involved in the decision-making. If she expresses a preference to exclude her parents, the physician should honor her preference.

wrongAnswers.A: “Do you want me to contact child protective services?" is not a question a physician should ask a patient. As a mandated reporter, the physician is required by law to report any suspected child abuse. There is no indication that the boyfriend or parents are abusing this patient or that this patient is a danger to the fetus.
wrongAnswers.B: "Have you considered placing the child up for adoption?" and "Would you like a confidential referral to discuss abortion services?" (Choice E) are leading questions that presume that one is the best option. The decision of whether to deliver and raise a child is a personal decision. The physician should facilitate discussion of the options while abstaining from expressing an opinion. "How do you think your boyfriend will react to this news?" (Choice C) strays from the physician’s role of facilitating informed decision-making about management options. Though the physician may encourage the patient to discuss the decision with her loved ones (including her boyfriend) so she can think through her decision, the boyfriend’s reaction is irrelevant. Additionally, this question may come off as judgmental.

questions.stem:
A previously healthy 82-year-old woman comes to the physician because of generalized weakness and a sore tongue for 1 month. She lives by herself. Her diet has consisted mainly of tea and homemade bread since her husband died 6 months ago. Examination shows pallor, mild jaundice, and a smooth, red tongue. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show:
Hematocrit: 26%
Mean corpuscular volume: 120 µm³
Leukocyte count: 2500/mm³
Reticulocyte count: 0.2%
Platelet count: 20,000/mm³
This patient most likely has which of the following nutritional deficiencies?
questions.stemHtml:
A previously healthy 82-year-old woman comes to the physician because of generalized weakness and a sore tongue for 1 month. She lives by herself. Her diet has consisted mainly of tea and homemade bread since her husband died 6 months ago. Examination shows pallor, mild jaundice, and a smooth, red tongue. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show:

Hematocrit26%
Mean corpuscular volume120 µm³
Leukocyte count2500/mm³
Reticulocyte count0.2%
Platelet count20,000/mm³

This patient most likely has which of the following nutritional deficiencies?
questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Folic acid, or vitamin B9, is converted in the body to tetrahydrofolic acid and used as a coenzyme in the synthesis of nucleotides and nucleosides. Folate is contained in leafy vegetables and primarily absorbed in the jejunum. Folate deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, and patients taking anti-folate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). Megaloblastic anemia occurs in the setting of impaired deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis, commonly related to folate or vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, and is classically characterized by erythrocyte macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils. Laboratory studies show anemia, increased mean corpuscular volume, and normal leukoctye and platelet indices. In this patient’s case, the megaloblastic anemia is likely a result of folic acid deficiency, as these stores in the body can be depleted quickly in cases of malnourishment, while vitamin B12 (cobalamin) reserves are substantial and take longer to deplete.

wrongAnswers.B: Niacin results in pellagra, which classically presents with the triad of dementia, diarrhea, and dermatitis. The dermatitis is generally seen around a patient’s neck in the pattern of a necklace. This patient has not had diarrhea or dermatitis. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) (Choice C) is a cofactor for several enzymes in glucose metabolism and adenosine triphosphate production, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency is characterized by Wernicke encephalopathy, a triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Wernicke encephalopathy is theoretically reversible with administration of high-dose thiamine; if untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome which is characterized by dementia, confabulation, hallucinations, and psychosis. Vitamin B6 (Choice D) deficiency is uncommon because of dietary insufficiency but when it does occur, it presents as glossitis, stomatitis, and seborrheic dermatitis. questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with dementia, Alzheimer type, is brought to the physician by her daughter for recommendations about driving restrictions. Since the patient moved in with her daughter 3 weeks ago, they have had several arguments because her daughter has not allowed the patient to drive. The patient last drove a car 2 years ago. She has no history of motor vehicle collisions. The patient's husband provided her daily care until he died of a myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. The patient's only medication is galantamine, which she has taken for 4 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status examination shows a sad mood and reactive affect. She reports no suicidal thoughts. She is able to correctly repeat six digits forward, and she recalls one of three objects after 5 minutes; she is unable to correctly copy a rectangle or two intersecting pentagons. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding this patient's driving?

She reports no suicidal thoughts. She is able to correctly repeat six digits forward, and she recalls one of three objects after 5 minutes; she is unable to correctly copy a rectangle or two intersecting pentagons. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding this patient's driving?
choices: The patient should be allowed to drive only with supervision
The patient should be allowed to drive short distances only
The patient should be allowed to drive until her driving skills are formally assessed
The patient should not have access to car keys until her driving skills are formally assessed
The patient's driver license should be revoked
questions.subject: Neurology

explanationPanel.correct: D. The patient should not have access to car keys until her driving skills are formally assessed
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Alzheimer dementia is the most prevalent dementia in elderly patients and is characterized by the loss of intellectual function within multiple domains. It typically presents with progressive cognitive decline that affects a patient's ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living before progressing to affect basic activities of daily living. Examples of instrumental activities of daily living include doing laundry, housework, shopping, preparing meals, taking medications, managing money, and driving. These are more advanced skills and require higher cognitive abilities than do the basic activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, and feeding. In order for elderly adults to remain independent in their homes, they must be able to perform instrumental activities of daily living. A patient’s ability to perform activities of daily living can be assessed with a combination of self-reporting, caregiver reporting, and direct observation (eg, driving test, occupational therapy evaluation). In the case of potentially unsafe activities (eg, driving), the unsafe activity should be restricted until formal assessment can happen. Formal assessments can reveal the need for in-home support or a move to an assisted living facility.

wrongAnswers.A: The patient should be allowed to drive only with supervision, the patient should be allowed to drive short distances only (Choice B), and the patient's driver license should be revoked (Choice E) are premature actions. No final decisions about the patient’s driving abilities should be made until her abilities are formally assessed. Until this assessment, she should be restricted from driving given that her driving may be unsafe. The patient should be allowed to drive until her driving skills are formally assessed (Choice C) recognizes the need for a formal driving assessment. However, this option introduces danger to the patient and society, as the patient may be an unsafe driver. The patient should be restricted from driving until her driving safety can be assessed.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old male infant is brought to the office by his parents because of a 1-week history of "increasing spit-up." His parents report that the patient will forcefully spit up within a few minutes after every feeding. He has a history of mild breast-feeding jaundice which resolved spontaneously. The patient was born at term following an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery to a primigravid mother. Vital signs are within normal limits. Palpation over the right upper abdominal quadrant discloses a 1.5-cm mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-week-old male infant is brought to the office by his parents because of a 1-week history of "increasing spit-up." His parents report that the patient will forcefully spit up within a few minutes after every feeding. He has a history of mild breast-feeding jaundice which resolved spontaneously. The patient was born at term following an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery to a primigravid mother. Vital signs are within normal limits. Palpation over the right upper abdominal quadrant discloses a 1.5-cm mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's symptoms?
choices: Anteroposterior and decubitus x-rays of the abdomen
Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel
Observation of the infant while feeding and spitting up
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings beginning around age 3 to 6 weeks, such as in this 4-week-old infant. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Repeated bouts of vomiting can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to losses of hydrochloric acid, a major component of gastric secretions. Infants can have severe electrolyte derangements that should be treated urgently. Dehydration can be shown on examination by decreased activity, listlessness, dry mucous membranes, and poor skin turgor. Pyloric stenosis on abdominal examination presents as a small, nontender mass in the epigastric region. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is by ultrasonography of the abdomen showing thickened pyloric musculature. Management includes correcting fluid and electrolyte abnormalities followed by surgical pyloromyotomy.

wrongAnswers.A: Anteroposterior and decubitus x-rays of the abdomen is a nonspecific study that would not necessarily show pyloric stenosis. An x-ray can help with the diagnosis of constipation and bowel obstruction but is neither sensitive nor specific. However, it would
wrongAnswers.B: not clearly outline hypertrophy of the pylorus. It would not be as helpful as ultrasonography of the abdomen for this patient with pyloric stenosis. Barium enema with air contrast is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine such as colon cancer. It can also be used in children to evaluate for congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Choice C) can be helpful in the full evaluation of pyloric stenosis and repeated vomiting, which can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. However, it would only be diagnostic of metabolic derangements and dehydration that can be addressed with supportive measures. Diagnosis and treatment of the underlying cause, pyloric stenosis, should be done using ultrasonography of the abdomen and surgical pyloromyotomy. Observation of the infant while feeding and spitting up (Choice E) can be helpful in determining between physiologic regurgitation in infants versus projectile vomiting in pyloric stenosis. However, this patient has a 1.5-cm mass on abdominal palpation, making physiologic regurgitation less likely. Due to palpation of an abdominal mass, further evaluation for pyloric stenosis should be done using ultrasonography of the abdomen.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks’ gestation comes to the office for her first prenatal visit. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her childhood immunization history is unknown. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccine to administer at this time?
questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks’ gestation comes to the office for her first prenatal visit. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her childhood immunization history is unknown. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccine to administer at this time?
questions.subject: Obstetrics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Routine immunizations indicated during pregnancy include the inactivated influenza virus vaccine and the tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine. The Tdap vaccine is typically administered between weeks 27 and 36 of gestation to optimize maternal antibody response and promote placental transfer of antibodies to the fetus but can be given at any time during the pregnancy. Before infants receive their own diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine at age 2 months, maternal Tdap vaccines protect infants against neonatal tetanus and pertussis, which are associated with significant mortality. To protect infants, patients should receive the Tdap vaccine during each pregnancy (even if the pregnancies occur within the same year). Regardless of gestational age, if a pregnant patient acquires a wound and has not yet received a routine Tdap vaccine during the current pregnancy, standard wound management measures should be adopted (eg, Tdap vaccination in patients with minor wounds who have not received a Tdap vaccine within the past 10 years).

wrongAnswers.A: Hepatitis B vaccine is recommended during pregnancy for patients who have not previously completed the hepatitis B vaccine series. Because this patient’s vaccine history is unknown, titers should be obtained to determine whether she has immunity to hepatitis B. If not, the vaccine should be given. Human papillomavirus (Choice B) vaccine is not typically administered during pregnancy. It has not been studied for its safety of administration during pregnancy. Because of this, it
wrongAnswers.B: Hepatitis B (Choice A) vaccine is recommended during pregnancy for patients who have not previously completed the hepatitis B vaccine series. Because this patient’s vaccine history is unknown, titers should be obtained to determine whether she has immunity to hepatitis B. If not, the vaccine should be given. Human papillomavirus vaccine is not typically administered during pregnancy. It has not been studied for its safety of administration during pregnancy. Because of this, it
wrongAnswers.C: is not a part of the recommended vaccinations administered to pregnant patients. Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella (Choice E) vaccines should not be administered during pregnancy. There is a theoretical risk that a live attenuated vaccine may cause the infant to contract the disease (eg, congenital rubella syndrome). Because of this risk, all live attenuated vaccines should be avoided during pregnancy.
wrongAnswers.E: is not a part of the recommended vaccinations administered to pregnant patients. Measles-mumps-rubella (Choice C) and varicella vaccines should not be administered during pregnancy. There is a theoretical risk that a live attenuated vaccine may cause the infant to contract the disease (eg, congenital rubella syndrome). Because of this risk, all live attenuated vaccines should be avoided during pregnancy.

explanationPanel.educationalObjective: The tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine is routinely administered between weeks 27 and 36 of gestation. This optimizes maternal antibody response and promotes placental transfer of antibodies to the fetus to prevent neonatal tetanus and pertussis. Tdap vaccination should occur during each pregnancy and can be given at any time during the pregnancy.

explanationPanel.trap: MMR and varicella are live vaccines and are contraindicated during pregnancy; HPV is deferred.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of daily expiratory wheezing for 2 weeks. She has also had an occasional cough during exercise and at night. She has had asthma for 2 years treated with inhaled albuterol. Examination shows bilateral expiratory wheezes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
questions.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of daily expiratory wheezing for 2 weeks. She has also had an occasional cough during exercise and at night. She has had asthma for 2 years treated with inhaled albuterol. Examination shows bilateral expiratory wheezes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Asthma is characterized by reversible obstruction of the bronchi secondary to hyperreactivity and airway inflammation. Patients present with episodes of wheezing, dry cough, and dyspnea. On physical examination, wheezes are heard and there is sometimes a component of prolonged expiration relative to inspiration. Chest x-rays are typically normal. Pulmonary function testing may be normal between symptomatic exacerbations, but during such episodes may show an obstructive pattern with increased residual volume and total lung capacity. The severity of asthma is graded based on frequency of day and nighttime symptomatic episodes. Intermittent asthma is characterized as symptoms occurring less than 2 days per week and less than 2 nights per month and requires as-needed, short-acting bronchodilators for symptomatic relief. Individuals with mild persistent asthma (such as this patient) exhibit symptoms at least 2 days per week or 2 nights per month, which requires the addition of daily inhaled low-dose corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone). Moderate persistent asthma is treated with the addition of inhaled long-acting β2-adrenergic agonists (eg, salmeterol) to the regimen of inhaled low- dose corticosteroids and, as needed, short-acting bronchodilator. Severe persistent asthma is treated with the addition of high-dose corticosteroids to the regimen.

wrongAnswers.B: Inhaled cromolyn sodium is a therapy that prevents mast-cell degranulation and the release of histamine from mast cells. It can be used in the treatment of asthma and allergic rhinitis. It is not the next step in mild persistent asthma, which is inhaled corticosteroids.
wrongAnswers.C: Oral leukotriene inhibitors, such as montelukast, are used to prevent smooth muscle contraction and airway edema in asthma. However, they are not as effective as inhaled corticosteroids in the treatment of mild persistent asthma. Thus, this patient with mild persistent asthma should be started on inhaled corticosteroids, which will be more effective in management of her asthma. Oral prednisone (Choice D) can be used for a short course in acute asthma exacerbations. For long-term pharmacotherapy, oral steroids are only used for patients with severe persistent asthma. This patient has mild persistent asthma, and inhaled steroids are the most appropriate next step.
wrongAnswers.D: Oral leukotriene inhibitors (Choice C), such as montelukast, are used to prevent smooth muscle contraction and airway edema in asthma. However, they are not as effective as inhaled corticosteroids in the treatment of mild persistent asthma. Thus, this patient with mild persistent asthma should be started on inhaled corticosteroids, which will be more effective in management of her asthma. Oral prednisone can be used for a short course in acute asthma exacerbations. For long-term pharmacotherapy, oral steroids are only used for patients with severe persistent asthma. This patient has mild persistent asthma, and inhaled steroids are the most appropriate next step.
wrongAnswers.E: No additional pharmacotherapy would not be appropriate in this patient with mild persistent asthma. In patients with mild persistent asthma, the addition of inhaled corticosteroids or similar appropriate controller agents is necessary. Patients with intermittent asthma may need no additional pharmacotherapy aside from short-acting bronchodilators, such as albuterol, as needed.

explanationPanel.educationalObjective: The management of asthma exacerbations is dependent on the severity of asthma. Individuals with mild persistent asthma exhibit symptoms more than 2 days per week or 2 nights per month, which requires the addition of daily inhaled low-dose corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone) to short-acting bronchodilators as needed.
explanationPanel.rule: Asthma symptoms more than 2 days per week or nocturnal/exercise symptoms indicate mild persistent asthma requiring daily inhaled corticosteroid.
explanationPanel.trap: Albuterol alone is for intermittent asthma; oral prednisone is for acute/severe exacerbations, not baseline mild persistence.

layer4.rule: Asthma symptoms more than 2 days per week or nocturnal/exercise symptoms indicate mild persistent asthma requiring daily inhaled corticosteroid.
layer4.trap: Albuterol alone is for intermittent asthma; oral prednisone is for acute/severe exacerbations, not baseline mild persistence.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a 4-day history of a severely itchy rash that started on his right hand and forearm but has since spread to his left hand. This morning, he noticed some "spots" around his waistline. Most of the spots are red bumps, but some of the spots now have turned into scabs. The patient's new roommate, who moved into his apartment a few weeks ago, has had a similar itchy rash. The patient has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the patient's right hand is shown; similar findings are noted over the waistline. There is no crusting or spreading erythema. He has no rash elsewhere. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?

Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the patient's right hand is shown; similar findings are noted over the waistline. There is no crusting or spreading erythema. He has no rash elsewhere. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Scabies is a cutaneous infection caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. Scabies is transmitted from direct skin-to-skin transmission from close contacts. Scabies classically presents with pruritic, superficial burrows and papules of the interweb spaces of the digits, flexural wrist, axillary folds, periumbilical area, waist, and genitalia. Scabies may be diagnosed clinically or following demonstration of mites on skin scrapings of affected areas using mineral oil preparation. Scabies is treated with topical permethrin applied from the neck down on two applications 1 week apart. To prevent recurrence, it is

recommended that patients wash all previously worn clothing and bedding in hot water, and dry affected clothing on a hot dryer setting. Additionally, any close contacts of the patient should be treated with permethrin to ensure successful treatment and prevent recurrence. Following treatment, scabies patients may experience pruritus for a few weeks, which is often responsive to oral antihistamines and topical steroids.

wrongAnswers.A: Oral acyclovir is the treatment for viral infections, including herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus. Classically, herpes simplex virus presents as a painful cluster of vesicles, which develop into superficial erosions on the skin or mucosal surface. Similarly, herpes zoster, associated with reactivation of varicella zoster virus, is characterized by painful clusters of vesicles distributed in a dermatomal pattern. Acyclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase, thereby preventing viral DNA replication, and is used to treat both herpes simplex and herpes zoster. Acyclovir is not used for the management of scabies infection. Oral cephalexin (Choice B) is a first-generation cephalosporin that targets gram-positive bacteria. The cephalosporin mechanism of action inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin binding proteins, inhibiting peptidoglycan synthesis of bacterial cell walls. Cephalexin is commonly used to treat skin pathogens including Staphylococcal sp. and Streptococcal sp. While cephalexin may be used to treat bacterial infections, it is not used to treat scabies. Oral prednisone (Choice C) and topical triamcinolone (Choice E) are glucocorticoids used to treat numerous inflammatory and autoimmune dermatologic conditions. Prednisone may be used for severe flares of inflammatory conditions like eczema or psoriasis; however, abrupt treatment withdrawal is associated with subsequent flaring of these conditions. Prednisone may serve as a bridge to alternative immunomodulatory pharmacologic therapies. explanationPanel.educationalObjective: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mite infestation, transmitted from direct skin-to-skin contact. Patients frequently present with pruritic papules and burrows found in the interweb spaces, intertriginous folds, and flexural surfaces. Patients and their close contacts must be treated with permethrin to ensure successful treatment and prevent recurrence. Following successful treatment, patients may experience itching for several weeks, which may be managed with antihistamines or topical corticosteroids.
explanationPanel.rule: Scabies causes intensely pruritic papules/burrows in finger webs, wrists, waist, or genitalia with close-contact spread; treat with topical permethrin.
explanationPanel.trap: Steroids or antibiotics may reduce inflammation/infection but do not eradicate Sarcoptes mites.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of low back pain that radiates to the left buttock and along the lateral side of the left leg. Her symptoms began 1 day after moving furniture in her home. She has not had fever, chills, constipation, or urinary incontinence. Examination shows diffuse tenderness over the paraspinal muscles of the lumbosacral area and no tenderness over the spine. Range of motion of the left lower extremity is limited by pain. Deep tendon reflexes are normal, muscle strength is intact, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

Deep tendon reflexes are normal, muscle strength is intact, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: CT scan of the lumbosacral spine
questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: This patient is likely presenting with acute low back pain secondary to moving furniture in her home. Nonspecific low back pain is a very common occurrence affecting the vast majority of patients seen in primary care. When treating patients with low back pain, it is important to conduct a thorough neurologic examination to evaluate for deficits in sensation or muscle strength as well as changes to deep tendon reflexes. It is common for nonspecific low back pain to present with referred symptoms such as pain radiating into the lower extremities without findings of neurologic deficit. Most patients with acute low back pain, or pain ongoing for less than 4 weeks, will have resolution of their symptoms without further treatment. Additional laboratory studies and imaging are often not necessary in cases of acute low back pain without neurologic deficits identified on physical exam. Red-flag symptoms which would indicate emergent imaging include new fecal incontinence, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, or rapidly progressive and significant neurologic deficits. In this case, because of the reassuring physical examination and the patient’s 1-week history of symptoms, the most appropriate next step in management would be oral ibuprofen therapy.

wrongAnswers.A: Bed rest for 1 week is not an appropriate treatment for acute low back pain. Patients who undergo bed rest have been shown to experience increasingly severe pain
wrongAnswers.B: and have a slower recovery. In this case, oral ibuprofen therapy is the most appropriate next step in management. CT scan of the lumbosacral spine may be a reasonable next step in management if red-flag symptoms such as new fecal incontinence, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, or rapidly progressive and significant neurologic deficits were present on exam. Typically, MRI is the preferred emergent imaging modality, but CT scan can be used if there are contraindications to MRI. This patient does not have neurologic deficits identified on examination, making ibuprofen the most appropriate next step in management. Epidural corticosteroid injection (Choice C) may be a reasonable treatment option for patients presenting with radiculopathy. Lumbar radiculopathy often presents as pain radiating from the lumbar spine into the lower extremities with the presence of motor or sensory deficits or changes in deep tendon reflexes. This patient is presenting with referred pain into the lower extremities without neurologic changes, making ibuprofen the most appropriate next step in management. Oral prednisone therapy (Choice E) can be used in cases of acute radiculopathy. However, evidence has shown that a short prednisone taper has limited -to -no benefit. In this case, the patient is presenting with 1 week of low back pain with referred symptoms in the lower extremities, making ibuprofen the most appropriate next step in management.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-week history of a recurrent and severely itchy diffuse rash. The patient reports that the rash typically resolves within 3 to 4 hours and is most severe over his back. He has not had fever, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or any other symptoms. Use of diphenhydramine during the episodes provides moderate relief. He has no history of serious illness and takes no routine medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient does not currently have a rash but shows a previously taken photograph of his back. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study at this time?

The patient does not currently have a rash but shows a previously taken photograph of his back. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study at this time?
choices: Complete blood count with leukocyte differential
No further diagnostic studies are indicated
questions.subject: Dermatology

explanationPanel.correct: E. No further diagnostic studies are indicated
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Urticaria or hives are characterized by transient skin or mucosal swelling associated with pink, pruritic wheals. Clinically, individual urticarial lesions resolve within 24 hours. Urticaria develops from mast-cell degranulation and subsequent release of vasoactive substances, including histamine, into the surrounding skin. There are multiple triggers of mast-cell degranulation, including allergens presented by IgE antibodies, substance P, C5a, and medications. Most cases of urticaria are idiopathic, although urticaria may be associated with upper respiratory tract infections, drugs including aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs), and certain foods. While hives are self-limited, symptomatic treatments include oral antihistamines, epinephrine in cases associated with anaphylaxis, and omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds IgE, in cases of chronic, refractory urticaria. No additional workup is required in the management of acute urticaria in the absence of other symptoms or presenting features.

wrongAnswers.A: C1-esterase inhibitor testing is used in the workup of hereditary or acquired angioedema. Angioedema is characterized by swellings in the dermis and subcutaneous or submucosal tissue. Angioedema commonly affects the larynx, lips, eyelids, genital region, and/or abdominal wall. Unlike in urticaria, cases of angioedema may last for 2 to 3 days. Triggers for angioedema include food allergies, insect stings, and medications including aspirin, NSAIDs, and iodinated contrast. While C1-esterase inhibitor testing is warranted in angioedema, this patient's clinical presentation is consistent with urticaria. Complete blood count with leukocyte differential (Choice B) may be utilized in patients with refractory urticaria when there is concern for a lymphoproliferative disorder or hypereosinophilic syndrome. Hypereosinophilic syndrome can be associated with the development of eczema, hives, or angioedema, in addition to end-organ dysfunction. Hypereosinophilic syndrome has been associated with F1P1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene, leading to a constitutive activated tyrosine kinase. This patient’s presentation is not consistent with hypereosinophilic syndrome. Radioallergosorbent testing (Choice C) is a blood test used to detect specific IgE antibodies. Development of IgE antibodies is associated with type I (immediate) hypersensitivity syndromes, which may trigger hives or anaphylaxis. Radioallergosorbent testing may be used to detect food allergies, pet dander allergies, and other environmental allergies. While radioallergosorbent testing may be used to test for potential allergens, it is not recommended in the workup of uncomplicated, acute urticaria. Serum C3 and C4 concentrations (Choice D) may be tested in cases of angioedema. Most cases of hereditary and acquired angioedema are associated with a decreased concentration of C4. Normal C4 concentration may be associated with idiopathic angioedema, angioedema associated with hypereosinophilia, and ACE-inhibitor associated angioedema. While C4 concentrations may be tested in the workup of angioedema, it is not recommended in the initial workup of urticaria.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. One year ago, her serum cholesterol concentration was 260 mg/dL, and she was started on a low-fat diet. She has no history of serious illness. Her Pap smears during the past 10 years have shown no abnormalities. Her last Pap smear was 1 year ago. Her mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus, and her father died of colon cancer at the age of 62 years. The patient does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She has been married for 15 years. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m². Her pulse is 64/min, and blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Preventive Medicine

explanationPanel.correct: D. Measurement of serum cholesterol concentration
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Increased serum concentrations of lipids, including low-density cholesterol, are associated with an increased risk for coronary vascular disease. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has recommended screening for hyperlipidemia in all men greater than age 35 years and in all women greater than age 45 years who are at an increased risk for coronary vascular disease. They also recommend initiating a statin medication in such persons age 40 to 75 years who are at an increased 10-year risk (greater than 10%) of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Other risk factors for coronary vascular disease include hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, a positive family history of coronary vascular disease, and smoking. Optimization of serum lipids with pharmacologic treatment and lifestyle modification can reduce the risk for coronary vascular disease and myocardial infarction. Statins remain the first-line pharmacologic therapy for most patients with hyperlipidemia. This patient should have her serum cholesterol concentration rechecked after implementing her lifestyle modifications 1 year ago, and if it is still increased, further interventions should be initiated.

The USPSTF recommends screening for abnormal blood glucose or diabetes mellitus in patients age 35 to 70 years who are overweight or diagnosed with obesity. Currently, fasting blood glucose or hemoglobin A1c measurements are more commonly used than glucose tolerance testing for initial screening.
